misconceptions.name: LEFT JOIN returns only matching rows
misconceptions.description: Treats LEFT JOIN like INNER JOIN. In fact a LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table; where there is no match the right-hand columns are NULL.
statements: a left join only returns the rows that match
left join is basically inner join
left join only gives rows present in both tables
misconceptions.check_question: Customer 7 has no orders. After `customers LEFT JOIN orders`, does customer 7 appear in the result? What do the order columns show?

counter_example.query: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
counter_example.explanation: Deepak Yadav and Meera Joshi have no orders, yet they appear — with NULL in the order columns. An INNER JOIN would drop them.

misconceptions.fix_hint: Count the left-table rows before and after the join: a LEFT JOIN never has fewer rows than the left table.

misconceptions.name: Filtering the right table in WHERE cancels the LEFT JOIN
misconceptions.description: A condition on the right table in WHERE removes the NULL-padded rows, so the LEFT JOIN silently behaves like an INNER JOIN. Put the condition in ON to keep unmatched left rows.
statements: i put the filter in where after the left join
where and on do the same thing in a left join
misconceptions.check_question: If you LEFT JOIN orders and then write WHERE o.status = 'delivered', what happens to customers who have no orders?

counter_example.query: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'delivered'
counter_example.explanation: With the condition in ON, every customer still appears; customers without a delivered order show NULL.

misconceptions.fix_hint: Move conditions on the right table from WHERE into the ON clause when you must keep unmatched left rows.

misconceptions.name: Joining tables without a join condition
misconceptions.description: Listing two tables (or JOIN without ON) pairs every row with every row — a cartesian product.
statements: sql will figure out how the tables are related
i just wrote from orders, customers
misconceptions.check_question: If orders has 12 rows and customers has 8, how many rows come out of `FROM orders, customers` with no condition?

counter_example.query: SELECT o.id, c.name FROM orders o, customers c
counter_example.explanation: 12 x 8 = 96 rows: every order is paired with every customer. The ON condition is what links an order to its own customer.

misconceptions.fix_hint: Always state how the tables relate: JOIN ... ON a.key = b.key.

misconceptions.name: Summing after a one-to-many join counts values more than once
misconceptions.description: Joining orders to order_items repeats each order's amount once per item, so SUM(o.amount) is inflated.
statements: joins dont change the totals
i joined the items table and summed the amount
misconceptions.check_question: Order 101 has two item rows. If you join orders to order_items and SUM(orders.amount), how many times is order 101's amount counted?

counter_example.query: SELECT c.name, SUM(o.amount) AS total FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.name
counter_example.explanation: Without the order_items join each order is counted once. Aggregate at the right level, or sum item-level values instead.

misconceptions.fix_hint: Before aggregating, ask: does this join repeat my rows? Aggregate before joining or sum values from the many-side table.

misconceptions.name: Multi-table joins repeat rows
misconceptions.description: Joining through a one-to-many chain repeats combinations. Use DISTINCT or aggregation when you want unique pairs.
statements: why am i getting the same row twice
my join returns duplicates
misconceptions.check_question: Aarav bought a Pen Set in two different orders. How many times does the pair (Aarav, Pen Set) appear after joining through orders and order_items?

counter_example.query: SELECT DISTINCT c.name, p.name AS product FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
counter_example.explanation: DISTINCT collapses repeated (customer, product) pairs.

misconceptions.fix_hint: Count rows at each join step; use DISTINCT only after you understand why rows repeat.

misconceptions.name: Comparing with NULL using = or <>
misconceptions.description: NULL means unknown; `= NULL` and `<> NULL` are never true. Use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL.
statements: where city = null
null equals null
i compare with null using equals
misconceptions.check_question: What does `SELECT 1 WHERE NULL = NULL` return — one row or none? Why?

counter_example.query: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city IS NULL
counter_example.explanation: IS NULL finds the customer whose city is unknown. `city = NULL` finds nothing because NULL = NULL is unknown, not true.

misconceptions.fix_hint: Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL.

misconceptions.name: <> 'x' also keeps rows where the value is NULL
misconceptions.description: A row whose status is NULL is neither equal to nor different from 'delivered'; a `<>` filter silently drops it.
statements: not equal to delivered will include everything else
status <> delivered gives all the other orders
misconceptions.check_question: Order 106 has status NULL. Does `WHERE status <> 'delivered'` include it?

counter_example.query: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status <> 'delivered' OR status IS NULL
counter_example.explanation: Add `OR status IS NULL` to include rows with an unknown status.

misconceptions.fix_hint: When a column can be NULL, decide explicitly what should happen to the NULL rows.

misconceptions.name: NOT IN with a subquery that returns NULL matches nothing
misconceptions.description: If the subquery result contains a NULL, `x NOT IN (...)` is never true. Use NOT EXISTS or filter NULLs out.
statements: not in always works
misconceptions.check_question: What does `WHERE 5 NOT IN (1, 2, NULL)` evaluate to?

counter_example.query: SELECT name FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)
counter_example.explanation: NOT EXISTS is not tripped up by NULLs.

misconceptions.fix_hint: Prefer NOT EXISTS, or add WHERE col IS NOT NULL inside the subquery.

misconceptions.name: COUNT(*) and COUNT(column) are the same
misconceptions.description: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) counts rows where the column is not NULL.
statements: count star and count column give the same number
count counts everything
misconceptions.check_question: Order 106 has no status. Will COUNT(*) and COUNT(status) over all orders give the same number?

counter_example.query: SELECT COUNT(*) AS all_orders, COUNT(status) AS with_status FROM orders
counter_example.explanation: 12 orders, but only 11 have a status.

misconceptions.fix_hint: Use COUNT(column) to ignore NULLs, COUNT(*) to count rows.

misconceptions.name: COUNT(*) after a LEFT JOIN counts the NULL row as 1
misconceptions.description: A customer with no orders still produces one NULL-padded row, so COUNT(*) gives 1 instead of 0. Count a column from the right table.
statements: count star gives the number of orders
misconceptions.check_question: Customer 7 has no orders. After a LEFT JOIN to orders, what does COUNT(*) return for that customer — and what should it be?

counter_example.query: SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS n_orders FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.name
counter_example.explanation: COUNT(o.id) ignores the NULL, so unmatched customers get 0.

misconceptions.fix_hint: After a LEFT JOIN, count a column from the right-hand table (COUNT(o.id)), not *.

misconceptions.name: Selecting a plain column next to an aggregate without GROUP BY
misconceptions.description: Without GROUP BY an aggregate collapses the table to one row; the plain column then shows an arbitrary value (or errors in other databases).
statements: i selected the customer and the sum together
sql will group it automatically
misconceptions.check_question: What does `SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) FROM orders` (no GROUP BY) return — one row per customer, or one row total?

counter_example.query: SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id
counter_example.explanation: GROUP BY makes one result row per customer_id.

misconceptions.fix_hint: Every non-aggregated column in SELECT must appear in GROUP BY.

misconceptions.name: Using WHERE to filter on an aggregate
misconceptions.description: WHERE filters rows before grouping, so it cannot use COUNT/SUM results. HAVING filters groups after aggregation.
statements: where count greater than one
where and having are the same
misconceptions.check_question: Which runs first — WHERE or GROUP BY? So can WHERE see COUNT(*)?

counter_example.query: SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
counter_example.explanation: HAVING runs after the groups exist.

misconceptions.fix_hint: Row conditions -> WHERE. Conditions on aggregates -> HAVING.

misconceptions.name: AND binds tighter than OR
misconceptions.description: `a OR b AND c` means `a OR (b AND c)`. Use parentheses to say what you mean.
statements: sql reads the conditions left to right
i did not use brackets
misconceptions.check_question: How does SQL read `city='Lucknow' OR city='Varanasi' AND signup_date > '2025-03-01'`? Which part is grouped?

counter_example.query: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE (city='Lucknow' OR city='Varanasi') AND signup_date > '2025-03-01'
counter_example.explanation: Brackets make the date test apply to both cities.

misconceptions.fix_hint: Whenever you mix AND and OR, add parentheses.

misconceptions.name: LIKE without wildcards matches whole values
misconceptions.description: `LIKE 'Pen'` only matches the exact text 'Pen'. Use % for 'anything': '%Pen%'.
statements: like pen finds anything containing pen
misconceptions.check_question: Does `name LIKE 'Pen'` match 'Pen Set'?

counter_example.query: SELECT name FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%Pen%'
counter_example.explanation: % stands for any number of characters.

misconceptions.fix_hint: Use % at the start/end for 'contains'.

misconceptions.name: LIMIT alone gives the top rows
misconceptions.description: Without ORDER BY the row order is not defined, so LIMIT 3 returns three arbitrary rows, not the 'top 3'.
statements: limit 3 gives the top three
rows come out in the order they were inserted
misconceptions.check_question: Is the first row of a table without ORDER BY guaranteed to be the highest price?

counter_example.query: SELECT name, price FROM products ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 3
counter_example.explanation: ORDER BY defines 'top'; LIMIT then cuts the list.

misconceptions.fix_hint: ORDER BY before LIMIT whenever the answer depends on order.

misconceptions.name: DISTINCT applies to just the first column
misconceptions.description: DISTINCT applies to the whole selected row, not to a single column.
statements: distinct city, name gives unique cities
misconceptions.check_question: What does `SELECT DISTINCT city, name FROM customers` make unique — city, name, or the pair?

counter_example.explanation: To get unique cities select only the city.

misconceptions.fix_hint: DISTINCT works on the full combination of selected columns.

misconceptions.name: AVG treats NULL as zero
misconceptions.description: AVG ignores NULLs: the average of 10, 20 and NULL is 15, not 10.
statements: null counts as zero in averages
misconceptions.check_question: What is AVG of the values 10, 20 and NULL?

counter_example.explanation: NULL values are skipped; use COALESCE(x, 0) if zeros are intended.

misconceptions.fix_hint: Decide whether a missing value should count as 0 and use COALESCE explicitly.

misconceptions.name: More indexes always make the database faster
misconceptions.description: Indexes speed up reads on the indexed columns but slow down writes and use space. They do not help every query.
statements: index everything
an index always helps
misconceptions.check_question: What happens to INSERT speed when a table has many indexes?

counter_example.explanation: Each insert must also update every index.

misconceptions.fix_hint: Index columns used in WHERE / JOIN / ORDER BY of frequent, slow queries.

misconceptions.name: Uncommitted changes are visible to everyone immediately
misconceptions.description: Inside a transaction your changes are private until COMMIT (isolation).
statements: as soon as i run update everybody sees it
misconceptions.check_question: Another session reads a row you updated but have not committed. Which value does it see?

counter_example.explanation: It sees the old value; that is isolation, part of ACID.

misconceptions.fix_hint: Think of a transaction as all-or-nothing and private until commit.

misconceptions.name: POST and PUT are interchangeable
misconceptions.description: PUT replaces a resource at a known URL and is idempotent; POST usually creates a new resource and is not idempotent.
statements: post and put do the same thing
misconceptions.check_question: If you send the same PUT twice, is the result different from sending it once? What about POST?

counter_example.explanation: Repeating a PUT leaves the same state; repeating a POST can create duplicates.

misconceptions.fix_hint: Use POST to create, PUT to replace, PATCH to update part of a resource.

misconceptions.name: 401 and 403 mean the same thing
misconceptions.description: 401 = not authenticated (who are you?). 403 = authenticated but not allowed.
statements: 401 is forbidden
403 means you need to log in
misconceptions.check_question: A logged-in user opens an admin-only page. Which status should the server return?

counter_example.explanation: 403 Forbidden: the identity is known but lacks permission. 401 means credentials are missing or invalid.

misconceptions.fix_hint: 401 -> prove who you are; 403 -> you are not allowed.

misconceptions.name: A GET request can be used to change data
misconceptions.description: GET must be safe and read-only; changes should use POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE.
statements: i can delete with a get link
misconceptions.check_question: Why is a `GET /delete?id=5` link dangerous?

counter_example.explanation: Browsers, crawlers and prefetchers issue GETs freely, so a GET must never change state.

misconceptions.fix_hint: Use the method that matches the action.

misconceptions.name: A Docker container is a full virtual machine
misconceptions.description: Containers share the host kernel and isolate processes; a VM boots its own operating system.
statements: docker is like a vm
misconceptions.check_question: Does each container run its own operating-system kernel?

counter_example.explanation: Containers share the host kernel, which is why they start in seconds and are lighter.

misconceptions.fix_hint: Image = recipe, container = running instance sharing the host kernel.

misconceptions.name: Attributes all actions to 'we' without clarifying own contribution
misconceptions.description: In behavioural answers, using only 'we' makes it impossible for the interviewer to assess what you personally contributed or decided.
statements: we did everything together
we handled the whole project and we resolved it
misconceptions.check_question: When describing a team achievement, how should you separate your individual actions from the team's?

counter_example.explanation: Say: 'The team's goal was X; my specific responsibility was Y, so I implemented Z.'

misconceptions.fix_hint: Use 'I' for your specific actions and decisions; use 'we' only for shared goals or context.

misconceptions.name: Omits measurable outcome or impact in STAR answer
misconceptions.description: Ending a behavioural answer with the task or action, without describing the result or what was learned.
statements: then we finished the task
so we wrote the code and that was it
misconceptions.check_question: Why is the 'Result' in STAR critical for interviewers?

counter_example.explanation: Without the Result, the interviewer cannot tell if your action solved the problem or improved any metric.

misconceptions.fix_hint: Always finish with what happened: error reduction, speedup, deadline met, or lessons learned.

misconceptions.name: Rambles without structure in self-introduction
misconceptions.description: Reciting entire life history or CV linearly rather than focusing on relevant skills, recent work, and why you want this role.
statements: i was born in and then went to school
my whole life story is
misconceptions.check_question: What is the recommended 3-part structure for a 90-second self-introduction?

counter_example.explanation: Structure as: Present (current focus/skills) -> Past (key project/achievement) -> Future (why this role).

misconceptions.fix_hint: Keep it under 90 seconds and focus on: who you are today, what you built, and why this role.

misconceptions.name: Describes project features without explaining personal role or architectural decisions
misconceptions.description: Listing what the app does without explaining architecture, trade-offs, and your personal responsibilities.
statements: the project has login and a dashboard
users can click buttons to view data
misconceptions.check_question: What should an engineer emphasize when walking through a project?

counter_example.explanation: Interviewers evaluate your engineering decisions, system architecture, and specific role — not just product features.

misconceptions.fix_hint: Lead with system architecture, data flow, your specific components, and a difficult technical challenge.
